title: How the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Works
dek: A 10-person gaming startup called Spawn spends 30 times more on tokens than payroll and has an agent fleet shipping 77,000 code changes a month. Its founder's two-year playbook is a field guide to what AI-native actually means, and why most companies will find it hard to copy. In the headlines: an AI startup bids for a bankrupt white-shoe law firm, and tech earnings expose a widening rift between hyperscalers and investors.

oneIdea.headline: Truly AI-native means tearing out the systems built for humans, not speeding them up.
oneIdea.summary: Most companies doing "AI transformation" use AI to do the same things faster, with an org chart someone from 20 years ago would still recognize. Spawn went the other way. It runs a persistent fleet of agents with names, memory and ownership of real functions. It killed pull requests, closed the feedback loop so player agents report bugs straight to the fleet, and turned two years of founder decisions into precedent that AI judges apply. Almost every breakthrough came from removing scaffolding designed for human work. What remains for humans is taste, deleting what new models make redundant, and supplying the ambition agents won't come up with on their own.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Precedent, not heroics
items.body: Spawn turned two years of founder decisions into written precedent that AI judges apply, escalating only the odd case to a human. General practice already works this way informally, through practice protocols and ICB pathways. Written, current precedent is also what an AI scribe or triage tool needs to behave consistently, so it is worth tidying our own protocols before asking software to follow them.

items.title: Where the loop closes
items.body: Spawn's product reports its own faults and a small model routes them. In a surgery the equivalent is a quick, low-friction way for staff to flag scribe errors, omissions and wrong codes, with someone reviewing them. Without that feedback the tool never improves and errors go unseen. The sceptical view is that Spawn's game has low stakes when something breaks, and a consultation note does not, so human sign-off on every note stays.

items.title: What the bills say about vendors
items.body: Heavy token spend and loss-making start-ups, the point Zitron presses, bears on who is selling us scribes. Prices today may be subsidised, and a supplier could change terms or fail. Ask about contract length, data export, and what happens to patient records if the vendor is sold. Healthcare relevance of the law firm and earnings stories is otherwise small.

the_other_side.text: Zitron argues that the AI boom is a chain of conditions that must all hold at once: ever-rising hyperscaler spending, growing AI revenue, cheap debt and continued venture funding. He claims roughly 80 per cent of the leading labs' enterprise revenue comes from loss-making start-ups burning heavily on tokens, and estimates customers consume two to ten dollars of tokens per subscription dollar. On his reading, a company spending thirty times its payroll on tokens is exactly the fragile, venture-subsidised demand that props up the revenue figures, not proof the model works. He wrote ten days before this edition and did not discuss Spawn.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether the value that agents create exceeds what they cost to run. Both accept as fact that Spawn spends about 3.1 million dollars a month on tokens, that hyperscaler AI revenue is growing fast, and that Amazon's cash flow is deeply negative. The empirical question is whether token spend of this scale is paid for by customer revenue rather than investor money; the observable is Spawn-like firms reporting profit, or hyperscalers disclosing AI revenue separately from capital spending. The residue is worldview: whether removing human scaffolding generalises beyond a ten-person company with a product its agents can observe. For Whittemore to be vindicated, other firms must copy the pattern and margins must hold. For Zitron, token bills must outrun revenue once subsidies fade. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore is bullish and anti-doom, Zitron certain of a bubble and anti-hype. The signal is that both treat compute cost as the fixed constraint, despite opposite priors. Watch whether Spawn, or its peers, publish unit economics.

headlines.headline: An AI law firm wants to buy a fallen white-shoe giant
headlines.summary: Weil, Gotshal & Manges, the 95-year-old firm that handled the Lehman and Enron bankruptcies, filed for Chapter 11. The cause was departing partners and a failed merger, not AI. Legal AI startup Crosby, last valued at $400 million with about 50 lawyers, has submitted a letter of intent for Weil's trademark, brand and internal data, and hopes to hire some of its 1,200 lawyers.

headlines.headline: A law firm's archive used to be worth zero. Now it's RL training data.
headlines.summary: Firms are thought to have almost no equity value once the rainmakers leave. But precedent documents, contract templates and workflows for elite bankruptcy work could be worth tens of millions of dollars to the right AI buyer. Lawyer Harneet K. pointed out that Google recently bid $10 million for Spirit Airlines' far less specialized operational data.

headlines.headline: Not everyone thinks the Weil data is buyable
headlines.summary: Gen Legal CEO Ryan Walker says his company looked at the deal and passed. His argument: the data belongs to the clients, the talent has already left, and it is better to recruit Weil attorneys directly. Crosby's investors at Lux and Index, meanwhile, are calling the bid a "master stroke."

headlines.headline: AI revenue is surging, and tech stocks are falling anyway
headlines.summary: AWS grew 39%, its best in almost five years, but Amazon's overall revenue and net income missed forecasts and the stock fell 6% after hours. Intel's data center business grew 78%, yet a soft forecast sent shares down 23%. Google dropped 12% in the day session, losing half a trillion dollars in market cap.

headlines.headline: Legacy businesses are paying for the AI build-out, and they're slowing
headlines.summary: Amazon is $42.4 billion cash-flow negative over twelve months. Intel's foundry is growing 58% while posting a $1.9 billion quarterly operating loss. The AI numbers in the filings don't point to a bubble, but if tech keeps sliding, expect the financial press to call it one.

headlines.headline: AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and 2028 and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to ten years.
headlines.attribution: Andy Jassy, Amazon CEO, on the earnings call
headlines.summary: The hyperscalers are not backing off. Analyst Andreas Steno Larsen calls it one of the fiercest battles he can recall between capital-market investors and tech executives who keep spending despite the market's objections.

headlines.headline: Democrats want Trump's Grok chats preserved as presidential records
headlines.summary: A Time profile reported that Trump asked Grok about the implications of forcibly removing Maduro. Reps. Raskin and Garcia, who could chair Judiciary and Oversight after the midterms, say chatbot logs are U.S. government property. They call relying on a "highly manipulatable and demonstrably error-prone" technology deeply troubling. The White House says it preserves all records the law requires.

headlines.headline: NYT: Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence asset
headlines.summary: The Times reports that an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, under U.S. surveillance on suspicion of diverting chips and passing information to Beijing, had a close relationship with Huang. Huang reportedly never received a defensive briefing. Nvidia says Megaspeed received only ordinary business information and that the diversion claims were debunked. The host's caution: the reporting is necessarily thin, but it comes from the Times, not a random poster.

headlines.headline: Most "AI transformation" is still the old company, just faster
headlines.summary: Most companies, AIDB included by the host's own admission, use AI to do the same things faster and better. Outputs stay similar, and the org chart would be recognizable to someone from 20 years ago. Spawn is what it looks like to drop the old startup rules entirely.

headlines.headline: Spawn's agents are persistent employees, not disposable tasks
headlines.summary: The 10-person game-creation startup runs a fleet of agents that persist instead of being spun up and torn down. Each has a name, an identity, memory and ownership of a function: game engine, bug hunting, even finance. The agents get Sundays off.

headlines.headline: $3.1 million a month on tokens, 30 times payroll
headlines.summary: That spend makes Spawn one of Anthropic's biggest customers. The fleet shipped 77,000 code changes last month, about 108 an hour. Founder Jacob Sanbury once assumed he was using agents wrong because his bills dwarfed what friends inside big tech were seeing.

headlines.headline: None of it worked until Fable
headlines.summary: Fable 500×'d the changes Spawn could ship, but the company had to rebuild operations around it. Sanbury's comparison: OpenAI's models game their own checks, Google's don't stay coherent long, and xAI's aren't smart enough yet. Anthropic's stay coherent and do the work, though he says their biggest weakness is not taking enough risk.

headlines.headline: Most companies run big human teams that use AI. We run a small human team alongside a big team of agents.
headlines.summary: A researcher at Anthropic told Sanbury that of all the customers they talk to, Spawn is the one that works most like Anthropic. Each day the fleet spawns thousands of helper agents for granular work, while the humans use a modified Claude Code for bigger-picture steering.

headlines.headline: Spawn killed pull requests because agents don't need the chatter
headlines.summary: Agents spent most of their time telling each other what they were changing, and doubling the agents roughly quadrupled the messages. Unlike specialized human devs, agents understand the whole system. So Spawn removed pull requests and lets agents work directly in the codebase, spawning a fixer whenever something breaks.

headlines.headline: Only ~1,000 reverts out of 123,000 changes, at a serious compute cost
headlines.summary: Test suites run every 15 minutes and the fleet has to have everything in line once an hour. The approach turns out to be surprisingly resilient, with no humans paged at 2 a.m. The cost is heavy: 5,000 CPUs, 17 TB of RAM and 150 GPUs on AWS, plus 60% surge capacity on standby.

headlines.headline: Take the human out of the bug-report loop
headlines.summary: Instead of humans relaying production faults to agents, players' in-game agents detect bugs and file reports automatically. A small model triages each report or feature request and routes it to the right fleet agent. The product is designed to be operated and observed by agents, which makes it close to self-healing.

headlines.headline: At Spawn, not shipping for an hour counts as an outage
headlines.summary: Because agents have limited memory and context, the system is more stable when it moves steadily than when it freezes and then lurches. In one typical incident, the issue was detected eight minutes after it hit a player, the cause was named a minute later, and a fix was live eleven minutes after that.

headlines.headline: 700 requests overnight led Spawn to turn founder taste into precedent
headlines.summary: The agents were finding questions faster than Sanbury could answer them, so Spawn formalized two years of decision logs into principles applied by AI judges. In the first eight days the judges made 11,000+ decisions: about 7,300 from precedent, 2,200 sent back to agents, 1,800 escalated to humans. Sanbury decided only 27, and daily shipped changes rose from about 1,000 to over 7,000.

headlines.headline: Engineers stopped owning systems. Now they're paratroopers.
headlines.summary: Humans drop into whatever situation needs them, get up to speed fast and unblock the agents. A big part of the job is taste, which includes telling Claude no even when something works. Another is deleting: in June, Sanbury scrapped six months of work covering 70% of the engine because a new model had made it redundant.

headlines.headline: Models build the next 2%. Humans have to ask for 100×.
headlines.summary: Agents are bad at noticing they've been heading the wrong way for days, and they won't propose radical ambition on their own. The prompt behind Spawn's best build yet came from the humans: how do you make a world a thousand times the size of GTA load on a phone in one second?

headlines.headline: Why big companies will struggle: you have to let agents break production
headlines.summary: Sanbury argues none of this works unless you close the loop, and that takes risk appetite. Humans break production all the time, since changes are the top cause of outages. In Spawn's experience, agents break things less often and fix them fast, as long as the loop lets them notice. With the right structure, every new model makes the whole company significantly better.

headlines.headline: Stop shoving AI into human-shaped boxes
headlines.summary: Spawn's agents handle customer support. They are sometimes a little wrong, but they answer right away and can act on the spot. When Spawn has taken them off support, customers got upset: they'd rather have an instant fix than a human who comes back two days later. Spawn doesn't pass its agents off as human.

headlines.headline: Two more reasons this is hard to copy
headlines.summary: First, a system like this is hard enough to build from scratch. If the host were replicating it, he would start a new division or product rather than retrofit an old one. Second, Spawn's self-healing depends on users' agents reporting bugs in real time, a feedback loop most products don't naturally have. The open question is whether you can design one in.

headlines.headline: Five lessons any team can take from Spawn
headlines.summary: 1) Give agents ongoing responsibility instead of one-off tasks. 2) Let the work carry the context through a shared, current record. 3) Make results observable. 4) Turn decisions into precedent, so each one also builds the canon. 5) Keep human attention on direction, because ambition and long-horizon thinking don't come naturally to agents.
